items.title: Trump’s Extraordinary Nvidia Intervention Sidelines National Security Concerns
items.summary: President Trump’s move to put Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia caps his indifference to the warnings of his own intelligence agencies.
items.full_text:
Title: Trump’s Extraordinary Nvidia Intervention Sidelines National Security Concerns - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-national-security.html

Published Time: Tue, 24 Nov 2026 01:03:58 GMT

Markdown Content:
By his own account, President Trump was watching the stock market slide and decided to stop it. He would take it upon himself to determine who should lead one of the nation’s largest companies. Never mind national security concerns, never mind the autonomy of the private sector. Mr. Trump would decide.

The president’s extraordinary intervention resulted in [Jensen Huang’s reinstatement](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-huang.html) as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced out amid a Chinese espionage scandal. Mr. Trump then got the result he sought. Sagging stock markets [shot back up](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/business/nvidia-stock-huang-ai-sp500-markets.html), restoring nearly $1 trillion in value alone to investors of Nvidia, who [happen to include himself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/technology/trump-nvidia-stock-purchases.html).

Everything about Mr. Trump’s handling of the scandal behind Mr. Huang’s fall and swift rise again has been astonishing: The president’s denial that he knew about Mr. Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset even though reports indicate [he was informed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/politics/trump-china-trip-nvidia.html) at least twice. His [shoulder-shrugging nonchalance](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/politics/nvidia-trump-huang-china-xi.html) about one of his tech lord donors in bed with an asset for a hostile power. And now his decision to bolster the wealth of investors over the warnings of his own intelligence agencies.

“I’m doing it for the country,” Mr. Trump [told CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/trump-nvidia-jensen-huang.html) on Monday morning shortly after Nvidia’s board bowed to his wishes. He explained that he had seen the markets collectively lose trillions of dollars in recent days, driven in part by the Huang scandal. “I watched that and, you know, I better get involved. If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”

Image

Mr. Trump has become personally acquainted with Mr. Huang and considers him an ally.Credit...Demetrius Freeman for The New York Times

The seeming trade of long-term national security concerns for a short-term stock rally sent shock waves through Washington, Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Even fellow Republicans, already unsettled by the Nvidia scandal, [expressed consternation](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/technology/republicans-trump-jensen-huang-nvidia.html) at the lack of accountability demonstrated by Mr. Huang’s quick return to the executive suite. Lawmakers in both parties cried foul and vowed to investigate.

“There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as ceo of the most advanced chip making company in the world,” former Speaker Newt Gingrich, a strong Trump ally, [wrote online](https://x.com/newtgingrich/status/2124893943636590926).

Senator Jack Reed, Democrat of Rhode Island and a member of the Senate Banking Committee that is scheduled to hear testimony from Mr. Huang on Dec. 3, said Congress should examine Mr. Trump’s communications with both Mr. Huang and the Nvidia board to determine what he assured or promised them.

“The administration’s top priority should be safeguarding our national security and ensuring America’s most powerful technologies serve the American people, not our adversaries,” Mr. Reed said in a statement. The economy, he added, depends on rule of law and fair dealing. “President Trump’s improper interventions damage these principles and must be investigated.”

As if Mr. Trump’s actions were not unusual enough, his public celebration of his successful arm-twisting only exacerbated the furor. Shortly after Nvidia restored Mr. Huang, Mr. Trump posted [a bizarre image on social media](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117666713950631493) portraying the once-and-future corporate chief executive as a martyr.

The image appeared to be an A.I. composite based on the famous photo of Mr. Trump after he survived an attempted assassination at a 2024 rally in Butler, Pa., surrounded by Secret Service agents, blood on his face, pumping his fist in the air. In the version that the president shared online, Mr. Huang was at the center of the frame, with blood on his face, holding up a red bra. Behind him waved a flag that said “Nvidia.”

The surreal post seemed to sum up Mr. Trump’s often flippant, from-the-gut, anything-goes approach to the presidency, in which his whims become official policy. With the image, he managed to mock both the seriousness of political violence and a major espionage operation all at once — flicking both off with a reference to women’s undergarments, as if it were a sexual conquest.

Image

Mr. Trump presenting Mr. Huang with a National Medal of Science in Washington last month. The president has written on social media that Mr. Huang was “a Great Patriot and National Treasure.”Credit...Demetrius Freeman for The New York Times

“You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks,” Mr. Trump [told The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-huang.html) on Monday morning.

As he has several times in recent days, Mr. Trump simply rejected the conclusions of his own U.S. intelligence agencies that the businesswoman involved with Mr. Huang was conducting espionage for China.

“Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy,” he told CNBC. But, he added, “with Jensen, I don’t believe that’s true.”

Whether Mr. Trump believes something is true matters more than contrary facts or investigations. His disregard of intelligence about Chinese interference in American affairs echoes his disregard of the intelligence about Russian interference in American affairs back in his first term. At C.I.A. headquarters in Langley, few have forgotten Mr. Trump’s [meeting in Helsinki](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/07/16/world/europe/trump-putin-election-intelligence.html) with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in 2018, when the U.S. president took the word of his Russian counterpart over that of his own intelligence agencies about Moscow’s meddling in the U.S. election in 2016.

At other times, Mr. Trump has seemed to accept that, in fact, perhaps the businesswoman involved with Mr. Huang really was working for the Chinese. But even then, he expressed no particular distress about it. “We spy on China, they spy on us,” he [told Fox News](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/trump-xi-shenzhen-spy-scandal.html) last week when he landed in Shenzhen, China, for meetings hosted by President Xi Jinping of China.

That, in turn, echoed his first-term equivalence when asked why he respected Mr. Putin, who was described as a killer. “We’ve got a lot of killers,” Mr. Trump said. “What, do you think our country’s so innocent?”

He continues to embrace Mr. Putin, with whom he met in Shenzhen. In another provocative social media message in recent days, Mr. Trump [posted a photo](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump?status_id=117656427563362319&attachment_id=117656427213859575) of the two of them shaking hands under the caption “My Friend,” touching off a storm of protest in Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe.

Image

Mr. Huang with Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan, in 2024. Mr. Trump denied that he knew about their affair even though reports indicate he was informed at least twice.Credit...Ann Wang/Reuters

The timing of the recent public disclosure of Mr. Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese asset proved uncomfortable for Mr. Trump, who was focused on his upcoming meeting with the Chinese leader. He made clear while in China that he had no intention of challenging Mr. Xi over the matter. While Mr. Trump said he did discuss the case “at length” in their private conversations, he characterized it not as a complaint about the espionage but a lament over the “tragedy” for Mr. Huang. China has denied the spying allegations, and the businesswoman has not commented.

Mr. Trump has been more aggressive about trying to steer the decisions of individual private companies than other presidents. He has pressured corporations to [eliminate diversity programs](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/23/business/trump-dei-corporate-reaction.html), sought to force [changes to pricing practices](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/20/business/trump-tariffs-price-increases.html) and asserted the power to [advance mergers that he favored](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/08/business/media/trump-netflix-paramount-deal.html). Among other things, he pushed Mr. Huang’s Nvidia last year to give the federal government a share of revenue on certain semiconductor chips to China connected to export licensing policy, essentially making the government a partner in Nvidia’s business in China.

Nor is Mr. Trump himself a completely disinterested player to the drama playing out at the company. He owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of last year, according to his [financial disclosure report](https://extapps2.oge.gov/201/Presiden.nsf/PAS+Index/405E4EC4E27BE8D185258DF7002DD1C0/%24FILE/Trump%2C%20Donald%20J.-05.08.2026-278T(2).pdf), and his brokerage accounts continued to buy and sell Nvidia shares as recently as September. Nvidia has also [donated $1 million](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/interactive/2025/trump-inauguration-donors-list/) to Mr. Trump’s inaugural fund and [at

items.title: Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia After President Trump Intervenes
items.summary: Mr. Trump, a close ally of Mr. Huang, led a campaign to assure the chip company’s board that the longtime chief executive did not present a national security risk.
items.full_text:
Title: Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia After President Trump Intervenes - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/nvidia-jensen-huang.html

Published Time: Tue, 24 Nov 2026 00:58:26 GMT

Markdown Content:
Nvidia said on Monday that Jensen Huang was returning to the chip-making giant he led to the top of the artificial intelligence boom, following a campaign led by President Trump that urged the company’s board of directors to bring him back.

After directing Vice President JD Vance to speak with Mr. Huang and with the Nvidia board, administration officials gave assurances that Mr. Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman identified as a [Chinese intelligence asset](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/politics/chinese-spy-agency-nvidia-jensen-huang.html), was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk.

Mr. Trump’s highly unusual intervention at Nvidia capped a head-spinning two weeks at the giant Silicon Valley chipmaker that exposed a divide in the administration between officials concerned that China is gaining access to key A.I. technology and others focused on the health of the stock market.

In the end, Mr. Trump, who has made plain he considers A.I. to be fundamental to the health of the U.S. economy, clearly sided with the stock market, which has slumped since Mr. Huang stepped down.

Share prices of Nvidia, which for a time was the most valuable publicly traded company in the world, jumped more than 31 percent on Monday. The S&P 500, one of the most widely tracked indexes in the world, rose 4.7 percent, the biggest daily gain since April 2025. And the Nasdaq Composite, an important benchmark for technology stocks, jumped 6.5 percent, reversing a last week’s steep decline.

Image

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/23/multimedia/23biz-nvidia-huang-stocks-tqlk/23biz-nvidia-huang-stocks-tqlk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Video monitors display news of the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, seen outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Monday.Credit...Angela Weiss/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Hours after Mr. Huang was reinstated, he made a triumphant return to the company’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters. Employees lined the company’s balcony and applauded as he entered. Some chanted: “Jensen! Jensen! Jensen!”

Mr. Huang clasped his hands together and bowed in gratitude. Then, he looked up at everyone cheering and put his hands over his heart.

“This is my first day of work,” he joked. “I don’t have a computer, so the I.T. department is going to give me a new P.C.”

Mr. Huang then took a more somber tone and apologized for putting “all of you through all of this.” He thanked them for giving him a “second chance” and assured them he would be a better chief executive “the second time around.”

“I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back,” Mr. Huang said.

Mr. Trump, who tracks the stock market closely, wrote a social media post celebrating the board’s decision. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he said.

But his return was widely questioned on Capitol Hill, with lawmakers from both parties asking whether the Trump administration was ignoring significant national security questions after revelations of Mr. Huang’s affair with the woman, Alice Huang, who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said in a social media post that Democrats would investigate “any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain” when they take control of Congress next year.

Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who is set to take over the House Intelligence Committee next year, said in a statement that Mr. Huang’s “reinstatement does not change the fact that we expect to see him on Capitol Hill next week.” In addition to Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, and Jeffrey Kessler, the under secretary of Commerce responsible for overseeing many U.S. technology controls, are scheduled to speak with lawmakers.

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina and the chairman of the Banking Committee, said he would also hold a public hearing on Dec. 3 at which Mr. Huang would testify.

Nvidia’s decision to restore Mr. Huang as chief executive came after Mr. Trump set in motion several days of behind-the-scenes maneuvering to pressure the company’s board, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Image

President Donald Trump and Jensen Huang at the White House in April last year.Credit...Pete Marovich for The New York Times

Late last week, Mr. Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his job back, the people said, despite concerns voiced publicly days earlier by his Treasury secretary about the possibility that banned high-end chips had been smuggled into China through companies purchasing from Nvidia.

Investors and former employees were also urging the board to bring back Mr. Huang, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private conversations. Some of them told board members that Mr. Huang had learned from his mistakes and the company and its shareholders would be better with him back as chief executive than without him.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations.

On Sunday night, Nvidia’s board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang’s reinstatement Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.

Mr. Trump has sought to separate Mr. Huang from the investigations into chip smuggling. But the Trump administration did not give Mr. Huang a so-called defensive briefing, a heads up that he was in a romantic relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

Image

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan.Credit...Ann Wang/Reuters

The Singapore-based company that Ms. Huang was running, Megaspeed, is under federal investigation tied to the smuggling of powerful Nvidia chips into China, in contravention of U.S. export laws.

Mr. Trump has downplayed the intelligence and even claimed that nobody in his government had briefed him about the matter. In fact, advisers to Mr. Trump, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, briefed him at least twice about the national security concerns surrounding Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang. (Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.)

The scandal turned China’s access to advanced A.I. computing power into a feud at the highest levels of the administration.

The debate set Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees chip policy, at odds with Mr. Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, who have all pushed to reinstate broad restrictions on data centers in recent months.

But his return created difficult questions for Nvidia’s board of directors, which just last week said that the billionaire had resigned voluntarily and that it had no intention of bringing him back. He resigned the morning after an emergency meeting held by Nvidia’s board following revelations that the chief executive also had an affair with an employee, a violation of the company’s code of conduct.

The board said in a statement on Monday that it had voted unanimously in favor of his return after “a series of discussions and meeting with Mr. Huang.” The board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”

Gavin Baker, managing partner at Atreides Management, an Nvidia shareholder, who is close with Mr. Huang, cheered the chief executive’s reinstatement. “Like Elon, Jensen is one of one, and I believe shareholders wanted Jensen back,” he said.

Mr. Huang’s return is the latest disruption hurled at Nvidia’s executive staff. Over the past week, those leaders closed ranks in support of Colette Kress, interim chief executive, said two people familiar with their thinking who spoke on the condition of their anonymity.

Many of the executives have been frustrated by the way Mr. Huang had inserted his family into positions of power at the company. His daughter, Madison, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, had been setting the company’s strategy for marketing, communications and business, and Mr. Caprez’s role as a leading dealmaker for Nvidia sidelined Ms. Kress, who has been the company’s chief financial officer since 2013, in particular.

Mr. Huang’s family members have continued to assert themselves. Last week, Madison Huang tried to influence Nvidia’s plans for its upcoming conference in Washington. The event was supposed to coincide with a briefing Mr. Huang is scheduled to give Congress. Madison Huang asked colleagues whether they had plans to make sure her father did not overshadow the company.

Mr. Huang made meeting with the executive staff a priority on Monday. He scheduled a meeting with them at 10 a.m.

Ana Swanson, Michael Go
